clean_story:
"Ink on paper. Printing History tracks its spread.

The name comes from the act of pressing ink onto surfaces to create copies, like a stamp duplicating its design over and over.

Most think of printing as books and newspapers, but its roots go deeper. The earliest known prints are cave stencils from 17000 years ago, where humans blew pigment over their hands to leave marks on walls. Later, the Sumerians carved seals into clay tablets around 3000 Before Common Era, pressing them into wet clay to mark ownership or trade goods. Woodblock printing in China around 200 Common Era used carved wooden blocks to print text and images on silk and paper, making Buddhist texts widely available. Johannes Gutenberg’s printing press in 1440 combined movable metal type, oil-based ink, and a screw press to produce books faster than ever before. A single press could create 3600 pages per day, turning books from rare treasures into everyday objects.

Three related subjects are papermaking history, movable type evolution and bookbinding techniques."
